791.quote_or_event: “To join oneself to many, and strive many days and examine dispositions, and take (for friends) those who are worthy, is proper. Even with a deadly serpent, to associate and afterwards to part from it will be painful.”
791.explanation: The Naladiyar tells the reader to examine people's dispositions over many days before taking them as friends, because once a bond is formed, even with something as deadly as a serpent, breaking it is painful.
791.tie_back: The Kural warns that nothing is worse than friendship formed without inquiry, since a loyal person cannot get free of it afterwards, and the Naladiyar makes the same point that examination must come first because parting later hurts.
791.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
791._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one with the Kural's argument (examine first, because release later is painful); Tamil Jain didactic text rather than canonical scripture.

792.quote_or_event: According to the Bhagavatī Sūtra, the wandering ascetic Gośāla attached himself to Mahāvīra and travelled with him as a disciple for about six years. He then broke away, founded the rival Ājīvika sect, and years later came to denounce Mahāvīra, killing two of his monks with a blast of fiery power (tejoleśyā) and hurling it at Mahāvīra himself, though it turned back on Gośāla.
792.explanation: Jain tradition remembers Gośāla as the companion whose long association ended in bitter enmity and death, a cautionary tale about close bonds with someone of unsound character.
792.tie_back: The Kural warns that intimacy with someone who was not examined again and again brings deadly grief in the end, and the Gośāla episode is Jainism's best-known story of a close companionship that turned lethal.
792.source: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti) 15, as retold in 'Association with Gosala' (jainworld.com)
792._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from a search check against the jainworld.com retelling and general reference accounts, not from a translation of the Bhagavatī itself. Thematically apt, but the Jain text does not draw the Kural's lesson about examining a friend beforehand. Next-best match.

793.quote_or_event: “A Sramana engaged in austerities, who longs for righteousness, should eat the proper quantity of allowed food, should select a companion of right understanding, and should live in a place suited to seclusion.”
793.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching on the path to liberation tells the monk to choose his companion deliberately, for that companion's sound understanding.
793.tie_back: The Kural tells us to make friends only after weighing a person's character, family, faults and associates, and the Jain canon likewise makes the careful choice of a companion part of the disciplined life.
793.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
793._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (Sramana written without diacritics). It shares the principle of choosing companions with care, but gives only one criterion where the Kural lists four (character, lineage, faults, associates), and it is addressed to monks.

794.quote_or_event: “Therefore, though the friendship of those who, like the channel which fructifies the rice-field, be ever so far away, we must nevertheless go to obtain it.”
794.explanation: The Naladiyar says the friendship of truly helpful people is worth going to great lengths for, however far away they are.
794.tie_back: The Kural says the friendship of a well-born person who fears blame is worth securing even at a price, and the Naladiyar likewise counts the right friend worth whatever effort it takes to win them.
794.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
794._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org (closing sentence of the stanza). It matches the idea of winning a worthy friend at a cost, but not the Kural's criteria of good family and shame at blame; Tamil Jain text.

795.quote_or_event: “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
795.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that hard words of correction are to be welcomed as a benefit, and that only fools resent them.
795.tie_back: The Kural says we should seek friends who can rebuke us sharply enough to make us weep, and the Jain canon likewise values the harsh word that corrects us over pleasant flattery.
795.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
795._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Shares the value placed on harsh correction, but the setting is a teacher and pupil, not friends, and the Kural's point about knowing the ways of the world is absent.

796.quote_or_event: “men will remain until they have done their work in an old house the thatch of which is untied, keeping out the water br a dam, and being drenched with the rain falling down upon them. Thus will friends! remain with one until their business is finished.”
796.explanation: The Naladiyar compares self-interested friends to workers who put up with a leaking house only until their job is done, and then leave.
796.tie_back: The Kural says misfortune is a measuring rod that shows how far friends really go for you, and the Naladiyar's leaking-house image likewise shows how far a fair-weather friend's loyalty reaches before it runs out.
796.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
796._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org; the stanza's opening address to the 'lord of the mountains' is left out, and the typos 'br' (for 'by') and 'friends!' are in the online text. It shares the idea that hardship exposes the limits of friendship, but does not present misfortune itself as a useful test.

797.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
797.explanation: Mahāvīra lists keeping away from foolish people as one of the essential steps on the road to final deliverance.
797.tie_back: The Kural calls giving up friendship with fools a person's true gain, and the Jain canon likewise puts avoiding fools among the requirements of the path to liberation.
797.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
797._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong match on avoiding fools; the Kural's commercial framing of this as 'profit' is absent, and the Jain goal is liberation, not worldly gain.

798.quote_or_event: “Avoiding the friendship of those who resemble elephants, seek the friendship of those who resemble dogs; for an elephant will kill his driver whom he has known for a long time, but a dog will wag his tail while the spear thrown at him is still in his body.”
798.explanation: The Naladiyar warns against friends who, like an elephant turning on its own driver, betray a long companion, and praises those who stay loyal even when wounded.
798.tie_back: The Kural forbids taking up the friendship of people who abandon you in trouble, and the Naladiyar likewise tells us to avoid such friends and seek those who stay faithful through suffering.
798.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
798._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org. Strong match on the second line of the Kural (avoiding friends who desert you); the first line, about spirit-shrinking thoughts, has no counterpart. Tamil Jain text.

799.quote_or_event: “if friends from whom it is difficult to separate, possess not virtuous dispositions, they are as a fire kindled to burn our hearts.”
799.explanation: The stanza says close friends who lack good character become a fire that burns the heart, because the bond is too close to break easily.
799.tie_back: The Kural says the memory of friends who deserted you in ruin burns the heart even at the hour of death, and the Naladiyar uses the same image of the heart burning because of unworthy friends.
799.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
799._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against wisdomlib.org (main clause of the stanza; the opening address to the 'lord of the wave-resounding shore' is omitted). Shares the heart-burning image, but the cause is a friend's bad character in general, not desertion in time of ruin, and there is no deathbed setting.

800.quote_or_event: “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
800.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching sets a high bar for companionship: a companion equal or superior in virtue, and otherwise solitude rather than company with someone unworthy.
800.tie_back: The Kural tells us to cling to the friendship of the blameless and to leave unfit friends whatever it costs, and the Jain canon likewise accepts only virtuous companions and prefers solitude to unworthy company.
800.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
800._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good fit for choosing only the blameless; the Kural's idea of paying a price to get out of a bad friendship is absent, and the verse is addressed to monks.
